q: Thin crescentic blade on an angled neck; cutting edge may be bevel-up or bevel-down.
u: Makes the sclerocorneal tunnel in manual SICS/phaco; also used for lamellar corneal dissection.
note: Crescent Knife — Identification: Blunt-tipped, bevel-up knife having cut-splitting action at the tip and at both sides. Its blade is curved and either mounted on a plastic handle (disposable) or can be fixed with metallic handle. Uses: Used to make tunnel incision in the sclera and cornea for phacoemulsification, manual SICS and sutureless trabeculectomy. Video note — Crescent Blade (Crescent Knife): Design: Blunt, rounded tip, beveled-up blade that cuts on both sides and the tip. Use: Used in Small Incision Cataract Surgery (SICS) to dissect the corneoscleral (sclerocorneal) tunnel and create a self-sealing tri-planar valve incision.

q: Thin triangular blade; usually forward-angled.
u: Enters the anterior chamber after the tunnel; may make the phaco corneal incision. Video 1 sizes: entry 2.8 mm (or 2.2 mm), extension 3.2 / 5.2 / 5.5 mm.
note: Keratomes — Identification: Flat, thin diamond-shaped blade with a sharp apex and two cutting edges. Uses: To make valvular corneal incisions for entry into the anterior chamber during all modern techniques of cataract extraction viz. phacoemulsification, SICS and even conventional ECCE and other intraocular surgeries, e.g. iridectomies and paracentesis. Video note — Keratome Blade: Design: Triangular, diamond/spear-shaped blade with a sharp apex and cutting edges on both sides. Use: Used to make the internal corneal entry into the anterior chamber (completing the third plane of the tri-planar incision). Sizes: 2.8 mm (or 2.2 mm): Standard Entry Keratome used in Phacoemulsification (where incisions are < 3 mm) and initial entry in SICS. 3.2 mm / 5.2 mm / 5.5 mm: Extension Keratome used to enlarge the internal incision in SICS or foldable/non-foldable IOL insertion.

q: Fine straight instrument with a triangular knife and cutting edges on both sides.
u: Makes the side-port entry at the limbus.
note: MVR or V-Lance Blade — Identification: Fine, straight but triangular knife similar to 15-degree side port entry blade but with cutting edges on both sides. Uses: Similar to 15-degree side port entry blade.

q: Long, thin, straight blade; maximum width permits passage of a 20 G needle.
u: Creates a side-port in cataract surgery for paracentesis, injection, second-instrument access and bimanual I/A.
note: 15-degree Side Port Entry Blade — Identification: Fine straight knife with a sharp pointed tip and cutting edge on one side. Uses: To make a small valvular clear corneal incision (commonly called as side port incision) in phacoemulsification and other intraocular surgeries including pars plana vitrectomy. Video note — 15-Degree Beveled Side-Port Blade (15-degree Lance Tip Knife): Design: Straight blade with a sharp, 15-degree beveled pointed tip. Primary Use: To make the side-port incision (paracentesis) at the limbus/clear cornea during cataract surgery (SICS and Phacoemulsification). Uses of the Side-Port Incision: During Cataract Surgery: 1. Injecting viscoelastic substances, trypan blue dye, or intracameral drugs. 2. Introducing micro-instruments (e.g., cystitome/capsulotomy needle, Sinskey hook/chopper). 3. Performing cortical wash (irrigation and aspiration). Standalone/Therapeutic Uses (Paracentesis): 1. Hyphema Wash: Washing out blood and clots from the anterior chamber following ocular trauma or surgery. 2. CRAO (Central Retinal Artery Occlusion): Performing an emergency paracentesis suddenly lowers the Intraocular Pressure (IOP), which helps dislodge the embolus to a more peripheral branch.

q: Flat handle with a short grooved neck; ophthalmic handle No. 3.
u: Accepts blade No. 11 (triangular) or No. 15 (curved elliptical); used for corneoscleral, trabeculectomy and skin incisions.
note: Scalpel Handle (Bard-Parker Handle) — Identification: It is a flat handle with a short grooved neck. Handle No. 3 is used in ophthalmic surgery. The blades fitted with the neck are No. 11 or No. 15 (No. 11 is triangular blade and No. 15 has curved tip). Uses: a) Ab-externo corneoscleral section for cataract surgery. b) Trabeculectomy operation. c) Skin incision as in DCR, ptosis or other lid surgeries. d) To dissect the pterygium head from the cornea. e) To give incision in chalazion operation. f) For suture removal after cataract operation. Advantages in cataract operation: a) It is a guarded section. As there is slow release of aqueous, the chance of quick decompression of the globe is almost nil. b) It is stepped, i.e. biplanar or triplanar incision - so wound security is better. Disadvantages: a) Easier for the beginners. A conjunctival flap is usually necessary before giving section. b) It is time consuming. User note on blades: Number 11 & Number 15 Blades — heading only in user's notes; these are the blades fitted to Bard-Parker Handle No. 3 (see above).

q: Spring with two limbs and an adjustment screw; can be used on either side.
u: Separates the eyelids, mainly for extraocular operations. Avoid routine use in intraocular surgery because pressure on the globe can raise IOP.
note: Pages note: Universal Eye Speculum — Identification: It has a spring and two limbs and a screw to adjust the limbs. It is called universal because it can be used on either side. Method: It is fixed to the eyelids in such a way that the screw should face outward and forward. Uses: It is used to separate both eyelids for good exposure of the eyeball mainly during extraocular operations: a) Pterygium excision. b) Squint operation. c) Evisceration and enucleation. d) Debridement and cautery of corneal ulcer. e) To give subconjunctival/sub-Tenon's injection. f) Removal of corneal foreign body. g) Removal of conjunctival cyst or mass. h) During suture removal. Disadvantages: a) Since it has no guard, eyelashes of upper lid (larger) come in the field of operation. b) Not used in intraocular operation because of more vitreous upthrust and risk of vitreous loss by pressure on the globe. Video 2 note (universal metallic speculum as described in video): Universal Eye Speculum: Heavier, solid blades (keeps eyelashes out of the field) with a screw lock; can be used for both right and left eyes. Used for extraocular surgeries (Squint, Pterygium, Chalazion, DCT/DCR, Evisceration, Enucleation) and Pars Plana Vitrectomy. (Video 1 also described the universal as thicker, solid blades with a screw mechanism, used in extraocular surgeries; the wire-speculum contrast — lightweight, thin wire blades, used in intraocular surgeries — is on card 8.) CONFLICT WARNING: These two sources conflict on eyelash guarding and on intraocular/Pars Plana Vitrectomy use — the pages note says the universal has no guard, so eyelashes of the upper lid come into the field, and says it is not used in intraocular operation, while the Video 2 note says it keeps eyelashes out of the field and lists Pars Plana Vitrectomy. The guarded speculum, not the universal, has the guard plate, and the pages note says not for intraocular use. Do not present both versions as true for the same instrument.

q: Upper limb has a guard plate that keeps upper-lid eyelashes out of the field; right- and left-sided versions.
u: Same general use as the universal speculum; particularly useful in children during squint surgery and in pterygium surgery.
note: Guarded Eye Speculum — Identification: The upper limb of the speculum is having a guard plate which keeps the eyelashes of the upper lid away from the field of operation. So two instruments are required, one for the right eye and the other for left eye. Uses: Same as universal eye speculum. It is specially useful in squint operation in children and in pterygium operation. Disadvantages: a) Operating field is reduced. b) It is heavier, hence gives more pressure on the globe. (For the full universal-speculum use list, see the Added note on the Universal eye speculum card: it is used to separate both eyelids for good exposure of the eyeball mainly during extraocular operations — pterygium excision, squint operation, evisceration and enucleation, debridement and cautery of corneal ulcer, subconjunctival/sub-Tenon's injection, removal of corneal foreign body, removal of conjunctival cyst or mass, and during suture removal.)

q: Light stainless-steel wire frame; no screw.
u: Applies little pressure to the globe, so the PDF notes it can be used in intraocular as well as extraocular operations.
note: Wire Speculum — It is made up of stainless steel wire and there is no screw. It is universal. It is very light and hence gives little pressure on the eyeball. So, it can be used in intraocular operation as well as extraocular operation. The speculum should not be confused with Muller's retractor, which has got two or three right-angle sharp-pointed pins (teeth) underneath to engage the skin flap. Video note — Wire Speculum (Barraquer): Lightweight, thin wire blades; used in intraocular surgeries. Video note (Video 2): Wire Speculum: Lightweight, exerts minimal pressure on the eyeball; used for intraocular surgeries (Cataract, Trabeculectomy) to prevent vitreous prolapse or IOP elevation.

q: Named and pictured in the speculum-design plate.
u: The PDF gives the name and image only; no separate description or use is supplied.

q: Medium-sized, fully serrated forceps with a catch; straight or curved.
u: Holds lid/bridle stitches and provides hemostasis, including during DCR/DCT if the angular vein is damaged.
note: Artery Forceps (Haemostat) — Identification: This is a medium-size, fully serrated forceps with catch. It may be straight or curved. The curved forceps are used more frequently. Uses: a) To hold lid stitches and superior rectus stitch, and then to fix the suture ends with head towel. b) To crush lateral canthus in lateral canthotomy. c) For haemostasis during DCR or DCT, especially if the angular vein is damaged. d) Fasanella-Servat operation of ptosis (to clamp conjunctiva, tarsal plate, Muller's muscle and levator muscle). e) To hold muscle stump during enucleation. f) To make irrigating cystitome from a 26-gauge disposable needle. g) To hold whole lacrimal sac prior to excision in DCT. Video note — Artery Forceps (Mosquito Hemostat): Design: Blunt tips with transverse serrations and a ratchet lock on the finger rings. Uses: Clamping bleeding vessels in lid/lacrimal sac surgeries, holding bridle/stay sutures, and crushing the lateral/medial palpebral ligaments or muscle bellies.

q: Stout forceps with an S-shaped double curve and 1:2 teeth at the tip.
u: Grasps the superior rectus for a bridle suture so the globe can be rotated downward; may hold the inferior rectus in keratoplasty.
note: Superior Rectus Holding Forceps — Identification: It is a stout forceps with double curvature (S-shaped) at its ends. It has 1:2 teeth at its tip. Its curvature at the tip is to fit with the curvature of the globe. Uses: It is used to catch the superior rectus muscle belly for passing stay (bridle) sutures, so that the eyeball can be rotated and fixed downwards in cataract, glaucoma or other surgery. It is also used to catch the inferior rectus muscle as in keratoplasty. Video note — Dastoor's Superior Rectus (SR) Holding Forceps: Identification: S-shaped (double-curved) shaft with 1x2 teeth at the tip. Use: Used to grasp the insertion of the Superior Rectus muscle (through the conjunctiva at 12 o'clock, ~7.7 mm behind the limbus) to pass a Bridle Suture (Stay Suture). Purpose of Bridle Suture: Fixes and rotates the eyeball downward to expose the superior limbus and sclera during cataract surgery (SICS/ECCE) or glaucoma filtration surgery (Trabeculectomy).

q: Small straight/curved forceps with long fine limbs, no teeth and a thickened tip platform.
u: Holds suture ends while tying and holds cut suture ends during removal.
note: Suture Tier Forceps — Identification: It is a small straight or curved forceps with long fine limbs. It does not have teeth at its tip. The tips are made stout by extra thick platform. Uses: a) To hold the suture ends during tying the sutures after proper tightening. b) To hold the cut ends of the suture during its removal. c) May be used to catch the margin of incised conjunctiva during suturing. d) To remove caterpillar hair.

q: Fine, medium-sized, toothless forceps with angulation about 7–8 mm from the tip.
u: Holds an IOL during posterior-chamber placement; can remove loose anterior capsule and act as a 10-0 nylon suture tier.
note: McPherson's Forceps — Identification: It is a fine, medium-sized toothless forceps with an angulation at about 7-8 mm from its tip. Uses: a) It is used to hold the intraocular lens during its placement in the posterior chamber. b) It is used to catch and remove the loose anterior capsule after completion of capsulotomy. Video note — McPherson Suture Tying Forceps & Ophthalmic Sutures: McPherson Forceps: Design: Fine, angled (or straight) non-toothed forceps with smooth, flat platforms at the tips and no lock. Uses: 1. Tying fine microsurgical sutures (10-0 Nylon or 8-0 Vicryl) in cataract surgery (when self-sealing tunnel architecture is inadequate), trabeculectomy, or corneal tear repair. (Note: A locking instrument is never used for delicate tissue/sutures as unlocking causes a sudden jerk). 2. Holding PMMA IOLs during insertion.

q: Fine, long forceps with a curved, sharp, toothless tip.
u: Performs continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC) in manual SICS or phaco; can remove a small capsular tag.
note: Utrata Capsulorhexis Forceps — Design: Long, angled blades with fine, sharp tips that meet precisely at the end to grasp the anterior lens capsule. Use: Performing Continuous Curvilinear Capsulorhexis (CCC) during cataract surgery (creates a smooth, tear-resistant circular opening in the anterior lens capsule).

q: Single-curved, toothless forceps with blunt knob-like tips and cups on the inner surfaces.
u: Grasps the lens capsule for ICCE; the PDF also lists removal of capsular tags, clots and caterpillar hair.

q: Straight, toothless forceps with slightly blunt tips and fine inner serrations.
u: Holds bulbar conjunctiva and episcleral tissue during dissection and conjunctival suturing.
note: Plain Dissecting Forceps — Identification: It is an ordinary straight forceps without any teeth at its tips. The ends are little blunt and on their inner surface, there are fine serrations for better grip. Uses: a) To hold the bulbar conjunctiva during its dissection. b) To hold episcleral tissue during its dissection. c) It is also used during suturing of conjunctiva. d) To hold conjunctiva during subconjunctival injection. e) It may be used to hold small sponge swabs.

q: Toothed tips are shown in the photograph.
u: The PDF provides the heading and photograph only; it does not specify identification details or uses.

q: Small, stout forceps with blunt flat ends and a thickened platform near the tip.
u: Removes misdirected eyelashes in trichiasis or the involved eyelash in a stye.

q: A needle-holding instrument is pictured under this heading.
u: The PDF gives the heading and photograph only; the detailed description and use are not specified here.

q: Notched tip.
u: Used to hold delicate tissues; the PDF notes that it is less traumatic.
note: Video 2 fixation variant note: This is the Video 2 fixation-forceps variant (Lim's / St. Martin's / Pierce Hoskins), added in addition to this Pierse-Hoskin card's original text, not a replacement for it. Lim's / St. Martin's / Pierce Hoskins Corneoscleral & Conjunctival Fixation Forceps: Design: Fine 1x2 toothed forceps at the tip. Uses: Holding and fixing the conjunctiva, Tenon's capsule, or scleral edge during peritomy, suturing, or globe fixation.

q: Medium-sized forceps with 2:3 teeth (sometimes 3:4) at the tip.
u: Fixes the eyeball during surgery; also used for bridle sutures, subconjunctival/sub-Tenon injection and forced-duction testing.
note: Added-note label: The existing card is fixation forceps (eyeball fixation forceps); this added note is the user's Lim's / St. Martin's / Pierce Hoskins fixation-forceps transcription — keep both, do not replace the existing card. Fixation Forceps — Lim's / St. Martin's / Pierce Hoskins Corneoscleral & Conjunctival Fixation Forceps: Design: Fine 1x2 toothed forceps at the tip. Uses: Holding and fixing the conjunctiva, Tenon's capsule, or scleral edge during peritomy, suturing, or globe fixation. Clarification: The existing card's 2:3/3:4 teeth describe the original eyeball fixation card/photo; the Video 2 Lim's / St. Martin's / Pierce variant described in the note above is 1x2 — these are different variants, do not mix the counts.

q: Small, fine forceps with long thin jaws and three interlocking teeth.
u: Used for grasping tissue in and around the eye.
note: Added-note label: The existing card is Bishop-Harmon iris tissue forceps; this added note is the user's general Iris Forceps transcription — keep both, do not replace the existing card. Iris Forceps — Identification: It is a small lightweight forceps with 1:2 teeth on the inner side of its tips. If the limb is closed, teeth cannot be seen or felt. The shape of the forceps may be straight, curved or angular. Method of Iridectomy: a) Hold the instrument in such a way that its tips face towards 12 o'clock position and angle towards 6 o'clock position. b) Now enter into the AC with closed tip and touch the peripheral iris. c) Open the forceps a little to catch a pinch of iris tissue and take out a triangular fold of iris outside the section. d) Cut a small triangular piece of iris radially with Wecker's scissors. Always check the severed iris tissue by rubbing it over face mask. This is to see if the pigmented layer has been cut or not, i.e., if there is release of pigment - it means iridectomy has been done in full thickness. Types of Iridectomy: 1. Peripheral button-hole iridectomy: (at 11 and/or 1 o'clock position) one full-thickness iridectomy is equally effective as two iridectomies. The indications are: a) In intracapsular cataract extraction (not mandatory in extracapsular cataract extraction). b) Angle closure glaucoma. c) As a part of trabeculectomy operation. d) In penetrating keratoplasty operation. Peripheral iridectomy is done to prevent pupillary block glaucoma and consequent iris prolapse in case of ICCE. As the aqueous can flow into the anterior chamber via this bypass channel, equilibrium between the anterior chamber and posterior chamber is maintained after ICCE. 2. Optical iridectomy: In case of central corneal opacity where facilities for keratoplasty are not available and rarely in polar cataracts. It is done in the lower part of the iris, as in the upper part, the new opening will be covered by upper lid. The best site for optical iridectomy is judged by stenopaic slit test, and it must be at the clearest zone. Customarily, it is said that the site of election will be down and in for the literates, and down and out for illiterates. 3. Glaucoma iridectomy or Iridectomy dialysis: Done in congestive glaucoma to facilitate drainage of aqueous. Here, iris is torn from its root instead of cutting it with the scissors. 4. Broad or Complete iridectomy: To facilitate the extraction of lens (combined extraction of cataract) when pupil is small and rigid, or if there is extensive synechiae, and if there is vitreous loss after cataract extraction. Indications: a) Iridectomy for prolapsed iris. b) Iridectomy to remove foreign body on the iris. c) Iridectomy to remove tumour or cyst. 5. Preliminary iridectomy: It is a test iridectomy, in uveitis causing complicated cataract, in the first sitting to see the reaction in that eye. 6. Involuntary iridectomy: It is the iridectomy caused by a cataract knife during 'ab-interno' section, when the AC becomes shallow or aqueous gets drained out early before completing the section. Here, there is no need for forceps or Wecker's scissors; YAG laser peripheral iridectomy is better in acute attack of ACG as it is a non-invasive (so no chance of infection) and cheap OPD procedure.

q: Large screw; one limb has a solid disc-shaped plate and the other a ring.
u: Fixes/evert the lid and provides hemostasis during chalazion surgery; can also secure the lid for intralesional steroid injection.
note: Chalazion Forceps — Identification: It is a forceps with a large screw for fixing or tightening the limbs like a clamp. One limb has got a solid disc-shaped plate and the other limb has a ring at its end. It is haemostatic and self-retaining. Method: The solid plate is applied on the skin surface of the lid and the ring side is applied on the tarsal conjunctiva, encircling the chalazion. The screw is tightened and the lid is everted and then chalazion is exposed for incision. Functions of the screw: a) Fixation of the lid. b) Haemostasis by means of tightening. Uses: a) To fix the chalazion for surgery and also to ensure haemostasis. b) To give intralesional injection of steroids in chalazion after fixing it with forceps. c) Excision of a small granuloma or papilloma of the lid. Video note — Chalazion Clamp: Design: Forceps with a screw lock on the handle; one tip has a flat solid disc (placed on the outer skin surface) and the other has a circular open ring (placed on the inner tarsal conjunctiva over the chalazion). Uses: Fixes the chalazion, everts the lid, and provides hemostasis. What is a Chalazion? A chronic, non-infectious lipogranulomatous inflammation of a Meibomian (tarsal) gland, presenting as a painless tarsal nodule.

q: Small scoop with a sharp edge attached to a handle.
u: Scoops out granulation tissue after incision of a chalazion.
note: Chalazion Scoop — Identification: Has a small cup with sharp margins attached to a narrow handle. Use: To scoop out the contents of the chalazion during incision and curettage. Video note — Chalazion Scoop (Meyerhoffer's Curette): Design: Small, sharp-edged cup/spoon on a handle. Use: Used for Incision and Curettage (I&C) of a chalazion. Surgical Pearl: A vertical incision is made on the palpebral conjunctiva (through the ring of the clamp) because the Meibomian glands run vertically in the tarsal plate; a horizontal incision would damage adjacent healthy Meibomian ducts.

q: Very small spring-action scissors; straight, curved or angular.
u: Used for fine ophthalmic cutting, including 10-0 sutures, conjunctival/trabecular flaps and iris.
note: Vanna's Scissors — Identification: It is much smaller scissors with spring action. It may be straight, curved or angular. Uses: a) To prepare conjunctival flap. b) To cut 10-0 sutures in cataract or keratoplasty operation. c) To cut trabecular flap in trabeculectomy. d) To cut anterior capsular tags in ECCE. e) To cut vitreous in open-sky vitrectomy, as in vitreous loss during ICCE or ECCE. f) To cut corneal button after trephination in corneal grafting. g) To cut iris in different types of iridectomy. Video note — Vannas Microsurgical Scissors: Design: Delicate, spring-action microsurgical scissors with very small, sharp blades (straight, curved, or angled). Uses: 1. Anterior Capsulotomy in cataract surgery (e.g., cutting capsular tags or performing envelope/can-opener capsulotomy). 2. Sphincterotomy: Cutting the pupillary sphincter in a small, rigid pupil. 3. Peripheral Iridectomy: Cutting a small piece of peripheral iris tissue. 4. Anterior Vitrectomy: Cutting vitreous strands in the anterior chamber following posterior capsular rent (PCR). 5. Cutting fine 10-0 Nylon corneoscleral sutures.

q: Fine corneoscleral scissors pictured on the page.
u: Enlarges corneal/corneoscleral incisions for ECCE, ICCE or keratoplasty; cuts scleral and trabecular tissue in trabeculectomy.

q: Spring-action scissors with fine, narrowed, blunt tips; straight or curved.
u: Used for conjunctival dissection and incising cornea, sclera and iris, and for dividing eye muscles.
note: Corneal / Conjunctival Scissors (Spring Scissors) — Design: Spring-action scissors with curved blades (longer and thicker than Vannas scissors; tips may be blunt or sharp). Uses: 1. Peritomy: Incising and undermining the conjunctiva at the limbus to create a fornix-based (cut at the limbus, reflected backward) or limbus-based (cut 8 mm behind the limbus, reflected toward the limbus) conjunctival flap. 2. Surgeries requiring Peritomy: Intraocular surgeries: Cataract surgery (SICS/ECCE), Trabeculectomy. Extraocular surgeries: Squint (Strabismus) surgery, Retinal Detachment (Scleral Buckling) surgery. 3. Enlarging the corneoscleral section in ECCE/ICCE and cutting sutures. (Example given in the user's video notes: Westcott's / Universal Corneal Scissors.)
